articles.text: Overnight training, school crossing-guard duties part of “service-in-lieu” agreement as DPRK eyes LA28 After four years of anticipation, the new Piedmont pool is set to open its doors on April 11, and the facility has already secured its first high-profile, if discreet, international tenant. City officials confirmed Wednesday an agreement with the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (DPRK) national diving team to use the aquatic center for intensive overnight training sessions ahead of the 2028 Los Angeles Olympic Games. Under a memorandum of understanding, the DPRK squad will have exclusive access to the competition pool from 9 p.m. to 5 a.m. nightly, operating in what staff described as a “low-profile, high-intensity capacity.” The team is expected to arrive via shuttle shortly after sunset and depart before the morning school bell, a schedule designed to keep specific training methodologies out of public view. Because international sanctions and currency restrictions complicate traditional lane-rental payments, the two parties settled on a “service-in-lieu” compensation model. In exchange for use of the pool and rooftop pavilion, members of the dive team and support staff will serve as uniformed school crossing guards throughout Piedmont during daytime hours.
articles.title: Piedmont Aquatic Center secures North Korean National Team as first “International” Partner

articles.text: On Sunday, March 28, Steve Kerr, coach of the Golden State Warriors, announced the team would practice at Piedmont High School and scrimmage with the school’s basketball team to ramp up for their NBA play-in game in the coming weeks. The Warriors believe the PHS basketball gym the perfect environment to refocus and prepare for a playoff push. The team has gone 5-10 in their last 15 games and is looking to shake things up by returning to a grassroots environment. After the Piedmont basketball team’s 19-9 season, the Warriors felt the Highlanders were ready to take on the challenge of playing with the pros. “They’re a great basketball team; they look ready to compete. We have to shake things up and use some unorthodox methods to refocus for a playoff push,” said Kerr. The Warriors practiced in Piedmont from March 30 to 31, scrimmaging twice on Tuesday. The team spent their Monday practice re-learning the basics with Piedmont head coach Ben Spencer. He helped the team with passing drills and helped Warriors shooting guard Brandon Podziemski learn how to pass to the open man. Reportedly Steph Curry played both scrimmage games AP Photo/Ben Margot Warriors coach Steve Kerr announces a practice bootcamp with Piedmont.

articles.text: The City appears to be fast-tracking another pool project. A second pool complex, is purported being planned to be built at the site of the old reservoir and is expected to be finished in just three months. The news comes as residents and city officials clamor over the beautiful new Moraga Avenue pool design and anxiously await the ribbon cutting ceremony just days away. The feasibility of another pool and the ambitious timetable at the defunct reservoir atop Blair Avenue come as a surprise to many. “With so much optimism in the warm spring air it sounds like the City is deciding to double down on the action and keep building,” said resident Poppy Smith. The Piedmont Post endorsed the first new pool complex’s construction initial Bond UU in the 2020 election. That $19,500,000 bond went significantly over budget and encountered many delays. As the sparkling new pool center promises to be one of the first all-electric pools in the country, more questions than answers arise about this second aquatics facility at the reservoir. Details on the new pool are still murky, but City employees were seen purchasing shovels and bags of cement from a local hardware store. “This is a head scratching decision,” said resident Hollister Quick. “But an extra place to swim would be nice during summer.” Blueprints on a napkin were obtained out of a Vista Avenue trash can by a resident. articles.text: Rory was found alone two weeks ago in the Oakland Animal Shelter parking lot and no one has come to claim him. He is a 40-pound Bulldog/Pittie mix with upright ears and a loving disposition. Rory is seven-years-old and hoping to leave the shelter and call a new place home. He takes treats gently, knows sit, walks nicely on leash, and jumps up beside you on the bench like he’s always been your dog. Polite when meeting other dogs, Rory keeps mostly to himself. He could do well as your one and only, or with an appropriately matched dog buddy. Come meet Rory at Oakland Animal Services this Thursday from 12 - 6:30 p.m., or this Friday, Saturday, or Sunday between 12 and 3 p.m. Rory is a 40-pound Bulldog/ Pittie mix Potential adopters with a child younger than 12 or a dog that weighs 25 pounds more or less than Rory must bring them to the shelter for the meeting. For more information about adoption or how to temporarily foster a puppy or dog, contact Piedmont resident Jessica McDevitt at jessicamcdev@ gmail.com.
articles.title: Adoptable Dog of the Week

articles.text: Gumbo is a gentle soul who’s saving his very best for someone patient enough to earn it. At first, he’s deeply shy—startled by sudden movement and unsure of new people—but someone thoughtful and steady will quickly notice there’s much more beneath the surface. This handsome lad likes to stay close, following his person from room to room and settling nearby throughout the day. He entertains himself with puzzle toys, wand play, and the occasional burst of catnip-fueled energy—but his favorite moments come when he feels safe enough to curl up close and sleep pressed against you. Gumbo takes time to build trust. He may hiss or retreat if approached too quickly, but someone who understands how to move slowly, read his signals, and let him initiate will be rewarded in a big way when he transforms into a devoted cuddle companion — flopping Adopt Gumbo through Cat Town. onto his back for gentle petting and seeking out closeness again and again. He’s done well in a calm, indoor-only home, and will sparkle his brightest with an adopter who sees the value in patience and quiet connection. Gumbo is neutered, vaccinated and microchipped. articles.text: The stairs and pathway through the former off-leash dog area in Linda Park are now open, and fencing around the park has been removed. The hillside remains closed, as re-vegetation is still in early stages. The City asks all visitors to stay on the path and keep both people and dogs, including on-leash dogs, off the grass, which is still fragile and easily damaged. The City is restoring the hillside as an oak woodland. A native California landscape that supports a rich mix of plant and animal life. Oak woodlands depend not just on trees, but on the grasses and understory plants below them that help hold soil, support insects and pollinators, and create habitat at different levels. While Piedmont’s parks contain many mature oaks, few areas are maintained as a natural oak woodland. As a naturally moist, northeast-facing slope, the Linda Park hillside makes an ideal location for this type of landscape. Along the path, interpretative signage provides information about the re-vegetation project and the value of oak woodlands. Restoration efforts are supported by a $5,000 donation from the Piedmont Garden Club’s Civic Improvement Committee, which provides funding annually for projects that enhance Piedmont’s beauty and ecological health. The funds will be used to purchase native understory plants for the hillside. The off-leash area was permanently closed last spring, after the Regional Water Quality Control Board notified the City that it needed to take steps to eliminate erosion and runoff from the hillside. Permanent closure and re-vegetation of the hillside allowed the City to address the problem and avoid steep penalties for noncompliance. After closing the area, Public Works “hydroseeded” the hillside. A technique that involves spraying the area with a mix of seed, water, and mulch. The mixture forms a protective shell over the soil, helping stabilize the slope while new grasses and other plants take root. Visitors are encouraged to enjoy the hillside from the benches, but should not walk on the grass under any circumstances. Staying on the path will help protect new growth and support the hillside’s long-term recovery. The Linda Park Hillside Visitors read interpretive signs about the oak woodland. articles.text: Oakland and Piedmont communities continue to search Amy Hillyard, co-owner of Farley’s East coffee shop in Oakland and President of the Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir, has been reported missing since March 25. According to the Oakland Police Department, Hillyard was last seen about 2 p.m. on March 25 near her home in the 500 block of Radnor Road in the Cleveland Heights area near Lake Merritt. Authorities said she did not have a cell phone with her. The Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir (PEBCC) released a statement on March 27 asking the public “to keep your eyes open in the coming days and stay aware of your surroundings,” adding that any information about the case should be directed to the Oakland Police Department’s Missing Persons Unit at 510-238- 3641. “This is incredibly difficult news for our close community. Amy is such an important part of our organization, and our hearts are with her and her loved ones as we hope for her safe return” PEBCC staff wrote. The Oakland Police Department and California Highway Patrol have released a Missing Person advisory for Alameda, San Francisco and San Mateo counties and are asking the public Amy Hillyard has been reported missing since March 25. to provide any relevant information in the missing persons case. Piedmont Police Chief Frederick Shavies said the department has not been contacted by the Oakland Police Department to assist with this case as of press time. “Based on the facts known to us at this time, this missing person matter does not fall within the venue or jurisdiction of the Piedmont Police Department,” Shavies said. “However, should the Oakland Police Department request assistance or investigative leads extend into the City of Piedmont, PPD stands ready to support as appropriate.” A candlelight vigil was held for Hillyard on March 29 at Lake Merritt. Friends and family gathered described her as a fixture in the Oakland community. “She really is a beloved community member,” Eric Tuan, artistic director at the Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir, told East Bay Times. “At the vigil it was said she would be the first person to organize a search like this if someone else in our community had gone missing.” Hillyard is described as a 52-year-old white female, 5’4” tall and weighing 120 pounds. She has blonde hair and hazel eyes. If you have any information regarding the whereabouts of Hillyard, please contact the Oakland Police Department’s Missing Persons Unit at (510) 238-3641.

articles.text: On April 11 at 6 p.m., Hill Branch of Children’s Hospital is hosting a special fundraiser, “April in Paris,” benefiting UCSF Benioff Children’s Hospital in Oakland. The evening will take place at Claremont Country Club (5295 Broadway Terrace) and promises a festive Parisian-inspired celebration. The event will feature live music, dancing, a silent and live auction, and hearty hors d’ouerves (the French word for appetizers). The hosts request that guests wear Parisian chic, but no denim. The fundraiser supports critical pediatric care and programs that serve children and families throughout the community. Hill Branch has a long-standing tradition of philanthropy, and this event continues its meaningful commitment to advancing children’s health locally. Hill Branch has raised over $7 million for UCSF Benioff Children’s Hospital. This money has funded important equipment and services that have saved the lives of thousands of children. Those interested may purchase tickets for $200. Drink tickets are available for an additional $15. There is an opportunity to become a sponsor of the event, with multiple tiers. articles.text: If you’ve been paying attention lately – especially if you have middle schoolers nearby – you’ve noticed: kids are showing up on e-bikes. Lots of them. Alongside self-driving cars, it’s one of the most visible changes in how our kids are moving through the world. And like most things that feel new and a little unsettling, it’s also a remarkable opportunity to learn together. Let’s start with the physics. The bicycle is one of history’s great inventions—efficient, mechanically elegant, and nearly unchanged in its core design for over 150 years. Part of what makes it so stable is that a spinning wheel naturally resists being tilted or pushed off course (you can feel this with our Bicycle Wheel Gyro Science Snack). Add a motor, and you have something that looks familiar but behaves very differently. Some e-bikes can reach speeds of 60 miles per hour. The machine can go 60—but that’s not the same as saying the rider should. Physics gives us the capability, but it’s up to us, as usual, to bring the This is where the conversation begins—not with rules, but with questions. Before your child gets on an e-bike, ask together: How fast is safe on a sidewalk? In a bike lane? Does the way they’re powered matter? What changes with speed—stopping A visitor takes the Bicycle Wheel Gyro exhibit for a spin at the Exploratorium distance, reaction time, visibility? Should helmets be required? E-bikes also add a new dimension to the question of commuting efficiency. They’re sometimes faster than cars in urban traffic—and sometimes not. Map a route together. Estimate travel times by car, bus, bike, and e-bike. Factor in elevation, traffic, and parking. These are the same questions engineers, city planners, and scientists ask, and your kid probably has opinions worth hearing. My kids and I have talked a lot about e-bikes, and their perspectives continue to surprise me and change how I think about them. They’ve long thought e-bikes are cool, but I was struck recently when one of their friends upgraded their e-bike to a scooter model that can reach speeds of 60mph, and they immediately announced it wasn’t safe. When I asked where the “line” for safety is—and for whom—we had a meaty conversation about sidewalk rights, permits, helmets, and even health care. Odds are your child has their own questions and opinions about e-bikes, and their answers might be more nuanced than you expect. Ask them what feels fair, safe, and practical—not just for them, but for everyone sharing the road, from cyclists and pedestrians to dogs and grandmas. articles.text: The Piedmont High School swim team delivered a strong showing against Berkeley on Friday, March 27, with the varsity boys securing a decisive 164–64 victory. The varsity girls fell 129–21, though the score line reflected a significant numbers disadvantage, as Berkeley fielded a much larger roster. Despite missing several key swimmers, Piedmont’s athletes rose to the occasion, many stepping outside their usual events and delivering impressive performances. Team captain Asher Takazawa, typically a backstroker, captured first place in the 100- yard butterfly with a time of 52.37. Fellow captain Cole Carnazzo, known for his strength in breaststroke, showcased his versatility by winning the 100 backstroke in 54.95. Teammate Ryan Mak followed closely, earning second place in the same event with a time of 56.44. On the girls’ side, the team competed without several top scorers due to injury and illness, including captains and key contributors. Still, Sofia Vuori led the charge, claiming first place in the 100 freestyle with a time of 1:00.28 and helping anchor the team through a challenging meet. Looking ahead, Piedmont will face Alameda High School in its next competition, which will also mark senior night at the newly renovated Piedmont Community Pool. As the regular season winds down, the team is gearing up for the high-stakes competition of the North Coast Section (NCS) championships and the CIF State meet, with hopes of advancing as many swimmers as possible. With resilience, adaptability, and strong leadership on display, Piedmont continues to build momentum heading into the postseason. articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ lacrosse team wrapped up a strong week by claiming a pair of wins over large enrollment schools. They beat Granada 11-10 in comefrom-behind fashion on Thursday, March 26 at Witter Field, and beat Cardinal Newman 9-5 in Santa Rosa on Saturday, March 28. “It was an intense game. We were without three of our starters and had to figure things out. We normally lose these close games, but we figured out how to win it,” coach Carlton Chan said following the win over Granada. The Highlanders have now won four of their last six matches after opening the season 0-5. Their win over Granada was a physical one, with Watson repeatedly taking hits from the Matadors’ overly aggressive defense. “They were very physical. It was the first game I’ve played in a long time where there was a lot of trash talking too. I was not expecting that, so it was definitely interesting to play a rough physical team,” said senior leader Peyton Watson. Watson took a hard tumble with 35 seconds left in the game that forced her to leave the action with PHS clinging onto an 11-10 lead. Freshman Sydney Latvala gained possession with 32 seconds left and resisted Granada’s press as the clock wound down. “I was just running around the field. It was stressful because we wanted to keep the ball to hold onto the win. My mindset was to just keep the ball and stay calm because it gets hectic when defenders are chasing you,” Latvala said. 11-10 victory over Granada There were three lead changes throughout the game, including Piedmont going up for good with 10:03 left in the fourth quarter. Both teams traded goals in the first quarter to make it 2-2 at the end of the first 12 minutes. articles.text: Many successful people say they don’t have time to exercise. But what if just a few hours a week could help you live longer and better? Investing time in your healthspan—the years you are able to stay active, independent, and fully engaged—is likely the highest-return investment in quality of life you can make. In fact, this is backed by scientific research. A landmark study led by I-Min Lee at the Harvard School of Public Health followed more than 650,000 adults for about 10 years. Study results were published in The Lancet (2012) and subsequently discussed in other medical journals. articles.text: Starting a fitness routine is hard. Finding the time is hard. Walking into something new can feel uncomfortable. And if you’ve tried doing it on your own—at home, in your garage, or following videos online— you know how easy it is to lose momentum. That’s where community makes a real difference. It helps you get more out of the time you put in and makes showing up feel easier. We’re built for community. Humans are social, and the people around us shape what we do. Research from MIT found that exercise habits can spread through social networks, meaning the active people around you can influence how much you move too. It’s not just about willpower. It’s about being in an environment that pulls you forward. That shows up in how hard you work. Group training research shows people often train at 10–15% higher intensity in a group, and in some settings exercise duration has increased by up to 200%. In practical terms, that can mean finishing the last 2–3 reps when your muscles start to burn, holding a plank or carry a few seconds longer, or adding five pounds instead of staying where it feels safe. Those small wins matter because they are what tell the body to build muscle and strength. Community also helps take the pressure off. You do not have to build the perfect plan or rely on perfect discipline. The structure is there, and the people around you help keep you moving. Research also shows people are 65% more likely to reach a goal when they commit to someone else. But this is not just about being active. It is about getting stronger. Muscle mass begins to decline after about age 30, typically by 3–8% per decade, and muscle power and performance continue to fall with age. At the same time, only about 24% of U.S. adults meet guidelines for both aerobic activity and muscle-strengthening work. That means most adults are not doing enough strength training to offset normal age-related decline. This is also why the first several weeks matter so much. Many people drop off early, and one study found dropout reached 47% within two months in an unsupervised setting. But the good news is the body starts adapting quickly: studies show meaningful neuromuscular changes and strength gains can happen in as little as 4 to 8 weeks of resistance training. In other words, if you can stay consistent through that early window, you are often right on the edge of feeling stronger, moving better, and seeing enough progress to make the habit feel worth it. We see this every day at BFT, where a diverse community of all ages trains side by side. Members say the same thing over and over: it is easier to show up when people know your name, encourage your effort, and are right there working alongside you. The workouts are one hour, structured, and simple to follow. You come in, train with your community, and get back to your day feeling stronger and more energized. That payoff shows up quickly. Even moderate exercise has been shown to increase energy by 20% and reduce fatigue by 65%. What starts as something you have to push yourself to do becomes something you just show up for—and that carries into how you show up for your family, your work, and your life. You do not have to figure this out alone. The right community makes it easier to start, easier to keep going, and much more likely that your effort turns into real strength, better health, and more energy for the people who matter most. articles.text: An exhibition showcasing the artistry of Lawrence Ferlinghetti, one of San Francisco’s most significant cultural figures, is now on view at the Legion of Honor. Ferlinghetti (1919 - 2021) was a poet, activist, publisher, and co-founder of the famous City Lights Bookstore in San Francisco, the epicenter of the Beat generation of writers. The independent bookstore is considered a literary landmark and has been a gathering space for writers since Ferlinghetti founded the store in 1955 with the now-famous Pocket Poets Series. Since then the press has gone on to publish a wide range of titles, including poetry and prose, fiction and nonfiction, international and local authors. Ferlinghetti was also an avid painter, draftsman, and printmaker, and his work across mediums often combines image and text exploring themes of isolation, violence, and human resilience. With artworks drawn entirely from the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco’s works on paper collection, this exhibition showcases Ferlinghetti’s work in printmaking, including etching, lithography, and letterpress. The exhibition is on view now through July 19. For more information, visit https://www. famsf.org/exhibitions/ferlinghetti-san-francisco. articles.text: The Fort Mason Center for Arts and Culture (FMCAC) in San Francisco is hosting this month’s Night Market, in partnership with Off the Grid and West Coast Craft, on Friday, April 17. The free monthly event in San Francisco runs on select Fridays from 5 p.m. to 10 p.m. April through December, and features live music, arts and crafts pop-up shops and hands-on workshops, as well as extended hours at nearby museums including Museo Italo Americano and FLAX Art & Design store on select dates. Fort Mason Night Market was conceptualized following the success of an inaugural night market in December that drew over 10,000 attendees. FMCAC hosts outdoor markets once a month through December that transform its iconic campus into a showcase of local artisans, cuisine, and live entertainment. Off the Grid provides more than 25 food and refreshment vendors at each event as attendees enjoy performances by local DJs, engage in hands-on creative workshops, and view public art installations from FMCAC collections. West Coast Craft, founded in San Francisco in 2013 to create a space for independent artists and designers to sell and promote their artwork, is hosted at FMCAC annually and is one of the largest arts fairs in the country. Local artisans who appear at the annual festival, which traditionally takes place in the summer, will be invited to sell their work at monthly Night Market events. “Fort Mason Center is known for being a gathering place, a space for people to exchange ideas, experience beauty, and connect with different modes of art and cultural expressions,” said Mike Buhler, FMCAC’s President and CEO. “We’re excited to collaborate with our partners to offer another way for people to come together, support local arts organizations and small businesses, and enjoy the natural beauty of the campus.” All events are free and open to the public. For more information, visit https://fortmason.org/event/fortmason-night-market-2026/ Live entertainment, arts and food vending take place at the iconic Fort Mason this month.

articles.text: Opera San Jose closes its 2025/26 season with Verdi’s classic opera La Traviata, premiering Sunday, April 19. La Traviata is an opera in three acts by Giuseppe Verdi, based on the novel La Dame aux Camélias by Alexandre Dumas fils. Opera San Jose’s production includes Mikayla Sager, most recently seen cast as the company’s Mimìs in La Bohème, as Violetta and former Opera San Jose Artist-in-Residence WooYoung Yoon as her young lover. Opera San Jose’s Former Conductor in Residence Johannes Löhner returns to make his principal conducting debut with inaugural Director-in-Residence Tara Branham returning to direct La Traviata. Set in 19th-century Paris, it tells the tragic love story of the courtesan Violetta Valéry and the young nobleman Alfredo Germont. After meeting at a party, Alfredo confesses he has long loved Violetta. Though ill with tuberculosis and accustomed to a life of luxury and independence, she eventually falls in love with him. The two leave Paris to live together in the countryside. Their happiness is disrupted when Alfredo’s father, Giorgio Germont, asks Violetta to leave Alfredo. He argues that their scandalous relationship threatens his family’s reputation and his daughter’s marriage prospects. Mikayla Sager, most recently seen cast as the company’s Mimìs in La Bohème, is cast as Violetta in Opera San Jose’s production of La Traviata. Sacrificing her own happiness, Violetta secretly agrees and returns to her former life without explaining why. The opera will be performed onstage April 19 through May 3. Doors open 90 minutes before the performance, 12:30 p.m. for matinees and 6:00 p.m. for evening performances May 1and 3 performances will be conducted by Conductor-in-Residence Noah Lindquist. A preshow discussion is held at 1:00 p.m. for matinees and 6:30 p.m. for evening performances. The organ player will be performing 30 minutes before curtain. articles.text: Free shows in Oakland, SF, Emeryville San Francisco Opera’s popular Bohème Out of the Box returns to the Bay Area this month, with free outdoor performances of an abridged version of Giacomo Puccini’s La Bohème at select locations in San Francisco, Emeryville, Oakland, Woodside and Concord. Launched during San Francisco Opera’s centennial season in 2023, Bohème Out of the Box is designed to bring opera beyond traditional venues and into neighborhoods throughout the region. Since its debut, the production has toured the cities of Alameda, Albany, Hayward and Los Gatos, as well as corporate and community sites across Silicon Valley. The one-hour production, performed on a converted shipping-container stage with piano accompaniment, opens April 11 and 12 at Crane Cove Park in San Francisco. Presented in Italian with live English translations available on mobile devices, the cast includes current and former Adler Fellows Alexa Frankian as Mimì and Edward Graves as Rodolfo, joined by Eugene Brancoveanu, Sofia Gotch, Gabriel Natal-Báez, James McCarthy, and Olivier Zerouali. The production will then travel to Christie Park in Emeryville on April 18, Henry J. Kaiser Center for the Arts in Oakland on April 19, Filoli Historic House & Garden in Woodside on April 22 and Todos Santos Plaza in Concord on April 25 and 26. Families are invited to attend free workshops 30 minutes before each performance, offering children an introduction to opera through movement and storytelling centered on Puccini’s music. Admission is free and seating is first come, first served. Registration is encouraged for most venues and required for the Woodside performance. The concert on Saturday in the Piedmont Center for the Arts was a benefit concert for the East Bay Center for the Blind. Judging by the size of the crowd, the concert was an overwhelming success. It was a “Schubertiade” because it featured the music of Franz Schubert. Concerts are something like boxing matches. There are the preliminaries and then comes the main event. The preliminary event on Saturday was a youthful work by Schubert, the “Sonatensatz.” Even though Franz Schubert was one of the greatest child geniuses of all time, this particular work was inconsequential. We were told that the composer wrote this piece when he was very young. There are many better works from the pen of the youthful Schubert. The performance featured pianist Ayaka Isono, violinist Maki Ishii and cellist Thalia Moore. I must say it was a rather lackluster warm-up, even though it was well played by the musicians. Then the floodgates opened and we were treated to one of the greatest compositions of all time - Schubert’s monumental Quintet for Strings. The featured players were violinists Maki Ishii and Michael Long, violist Paul Ehrlich, and cellists Victoria Ehrlich and Thalia Moore. The concert was arranged but Paganini was very disappointed that Beethoven had died the previous year. articles.text: One of the rewarding pleasures of movies is seeing one with friends, and then chatting about it when the lights come up. The Piedmont Flix Fest meets on the second Thursday of each month, offering a great movie in a comfortable setting, followed by a lively discussion. The Flix Fest April selection is an Academy Award-winning book-tofilm adaptation of the 1922 novel by Elizabeth von Arnim titled Enchanted April. The movie will be screened on Thursday, April 9, at the Piedmont Center of the Arts on 801 Magnolia Avenue. Doors will open at 3:45 p.m., and the movie is free for anyone 18 years or older. Participants are invited on a drop-in basis and can bring snacks. The movie’s opening scene takes us to post-WWI London on a dreary, rainy day, when Lottie Wilkins (Josie Lawrence) spots a newspaper ad advertising a castle in Italy with ‘sunshine and wisteria’ available to rent for the month of April. Seeking an escape from her loveless marriage and mundane life, Lottie invites her friend, Rose (Miranda Richardson), to join her in renting the Castello San Salvatore above the town of Portofino. To share the castle’s expense, Lottie and Rose invite a socialite, Lady Caroline Hester (Polly Walker), and aging dowager Mrs. Fisher (Joan Plowright), to join them in this ladiesonly adventure! The castle’s stunning scenery and the beauty of its lush flora enchant the women and help them begin a process of rediscovery. Lottie and Rose invite their husbands to join them, and each enjoys a renewal of their marriage that had atrophied in London. Lady Caroline escapes the obsessive male attention of her privileged social life and finds true romance from her surprising connection to the castle’s owner. Lastly, Mrs. Fisher finds wonderful friendships with each of the other women, helping shed her preoccupation with her Victorina past. In the movie’s last scene, she gives an emphatic symbol for this change when she drives her walking stick into the muddy path, leaving it and her past behind. The next movie will be Ramen Girl, a 2008 comedy to be shown on May 14 at the normal time of 1 p.m. Polly Walker in Enchanted April.

articles.text: James Suckling’s tasting featured over 200 wineries from around the world. San Francisco’s wine scene took center stage on March 8, 2026, as internationally renowned critic James Suckling brought his “Great Wines of the World” tasting tour to the city’s scenic Fort Mason Center. The event, part of a three-city U.S. series, served as a vibrant finale and drew wine professionals, collectors, and enthusiasts from across the country. Held at the Gateway Pavilion overlooking San Francisco Bay, the tasting offered a sweeping snapshot of the global wine landscape. More than 200 producers poured over 400 wines from 35 regions, spanning Bordeaux, Burgundy, Tuscany, and Piedmont, alongside top estates from California, Oregon, and Washington, as well as emerging producers from South America. The event’s format encouraged both discovery and dialogue. Attendees moved through a lively walk-around tasting, sampling wines that had all received 92 points or higher, including numerous bottles rated close to perfection. The opportunity to speak directly with winemakers and estate owners added depth to the experience, transforming it from a simple tasting into a forum for exchange about vintages, vineyard practices, and global market trends. With approximately 2,500 attendees at the San Francisco stop, the event highlighted the Bay Area’s importance as both a cultural hub and a key market for fine wine. Beyond the numbers, however, the tasting reflected broader industry conversations – how to engage new consumers, sustain interest in premium wines, and navigate a changing global marketplace. Ultimately, the March 8 tasting was more than a showcase of exceptional bottles. It was a celebration of wine as a global language – one that connects regions, traditions, and people. Under Suckling’s curatorial eye, San Francisco once again proved itself a vital crossroads for the world of wine. This was a tasting of wines that had already shown they were winners, but at any large tasting like this, some wines that stand out at the end of the day – wines you do not forget. The wines reviewed below are those unforgettable wines. They are the Cream of the Cream of the crop. The tasting filled the Grand Pavilion at Fort Mason in San Francisco.

The mid-palate is silky and direct, quickly gaining momentum, power and delineation. Equal parts fresh and tenacious, this has immediate appeal while displaying all the hallmarks of a long life in the cellar. articles.text: It was a warm, sunny March afternoon when Cub Scout Den 7, Pack 3 and parents set out into Henry W. Coe State Park on the thin dirt trail leading to our campsite. Our hefty backpacks held all our supplies for the next few days – tents, sleeping bags, food and water, first aid kits, pots, and camp stoves. It was hard, hiking with the heavy backpacks and it was easy to slip on some loose pebbles and lose our balance. Nevertheless, the hike was beautiful, with spectacular sights at every turn, like the bench overlooking a vast, majestic valley. Other times we were surrounded by towering trees. I felt so connected to nature. It was just us on the trail – nobody but ourselves and the trees. We had planned to stay at the Manzanita Point Group Camp, but once we got there we decided to keep hiking. Even with the filters that we brought along with us, the water in the nearby pond was too dirty to use. To get to the clearing where we would spend the night, we had to hike another mile and a half, cross a stream, and push through a few bushes. Some of us stumbled back down the thin poison oak-covered trail to the creek near our campsite to filter the water that we would use to cook dinner. After we had boiled the water, we poured it into bags of dehydrated food and waited. When we opened the dry food, it didn’t look very good. It was wrinkled and covered in powder, but with the water, suddenly it looked normal. The food wasn’t necessarily the best, but it was warm, and it filled us up. Because our food would be eaten by hungry animals if we left it out, one of the parents put it in a bag and hung it from a tree branch. Because they needed to be small and light enough to carry, our tents were a little cramped. Also, because we were so far away from our busy modern world, the animals were louder than I’d heard before. The next morning, after waking up and Piedmont Pack 3, Den 7 fifth graders and parents, at the end of their weekend backpacking trip in Henry W. Coe State Park. having breakfast, our group set out to China Hole to go swimming. The water was cold, but we got used to it quickly. One of us even found some small animal bones in the water. We noticed that there were some good skipping rocks, and so most of the time we were there we were skipping the rocks. We also found a piece of driftwood that worked better than most of the rocks. After getting out of the water we ate a meal of mainly snack food. We hiked back to our campsite and started stuffing our supplies into our bags to get ready to move. We had enough water to last the rest of our trip, and we wanted to make the final hike back a little bit easier, so we hiked up the hill to Manzanita Point campground, where we had originally planned to stay. One of the scouts brought a hammock which we tied between two trees and took turns swinging each other fast. After a relaxing night of stargazing, some of us brought out our lanterns to play card games at the picnic table. We retreated to our tents for the night. When we woke up, we had to pack again. We made our final hike back to our cars on a road instead of a trail and at one point, we were all tired of walking. When we got back to our cars, we took a picture with all our gear on, signaling the end of our backpacking trip. Even if there was some pain along the way, it was an amazing first backpacking experience. It was also our last trip as Cub Scouts, after all these years together we were splitting up and going our separate ways. I’m glad that we went out with a bang. articles.text: A veteran from USS Hornet, he served on ship as volunteer docent Joseph Leather, a long time Piedmont resident, passed away on March 14, 2026 in his home with his family by his side. Joe was born in Ecorse, Michigan on August 4, 1932. He enlisted in the Navy following graduation from high school and was stationed on the USS Philippine Sea and USS Hornet during the Korean War. While in the Navy he met his future wife on a blind date. They married on February 9, 1957, and shared 69 years together. Following his discharge from the Navy in 1956, Joe began working for United Airlines at the San Francisco Maintenance base. He began as a mechanic and went on to become an inspector and later supervisor in the engine shop. He enjoyed his work at United and dedicated 39 years to the company. Wilma and Joe visited England multiple times and traveled all around Europe and Japan as they visited their daughter and son-in-law who lived in multiple locations. When the USS Hornet was brought to Alameda to be restored, he immediately volunteered. He worked with the Duct crew repairing areas throughout the ship. As the ship opened to the public, he became a docent. He enjoyed giving tours and meeting people from different locations. Having served on the USS Hornet, the ship became his second home for 25 years. Working with other volunteers, he took great pride in bringing the ship back to life. He served on the Docent Board and contributed many hours to special events. He loved his ship and was proud of the role he played in preserving an important part of our history. Joe loved the outdoors and in the last few years he became an avid bird watcher. He enjoyed watching the birds build a nest in his bird house, and was quite excited about the eagles nesting nearby in the cemetery. He belonged to the Oakland Casting Club, Veterans of Foreign Wars, and United Retiree group. He Joe Leather, a veteran of the Korean War, died on March 14 at age 94. loved fishing and tying flies. A military graveside service was held on March 20, 2026, in Mountain View Cemetery. Joe is survived by his wife, Wilma, and daughters Carol Stellman and husband Robert; and Linda Collett and husband David. He is also survived by five grandchildren, Marie Stellman, Diana Stellman, Bradford Collett, Nathaniel Collett, Brenton Collett, and four wonderful great grandchildren, Charlie Collett, Oliver Collett, Henry Collett and Liam Collett. In lieu of flowers, he preferred memorial gifts to the USS Hornet Museum, P.O. Box 460; Alameda, CA 94501.

articles.text: As the April 11 opening of the new Community Pool nears, the City is adding more time-limited parking and increasing parking enforcement in the Civic Center. The goal is to keep short-term parking available for people visiting the pool and other Civic Center destinations, including City Hall, Veterans Hall, school sites, the Alan Harvey Theater, Piedmont Center for the Arts, and local businesses. Starting the week of April 6, parking on Bonita Avenue between Magnolia and Vista Avenues that currently is unrestricted will become time-limited, primarily 2-hour spaces. Some employee parking spaces on Magnolia Avenue are being converted to 2-hour visitor parking. Three new ADA parking spaces will be marked. Two in front of the pool entrance, and one in front of the Corey Riech Tennis Center. Cumulatively, these changes will more than double short-term parking along Magnolia, Bonita, and Vista Avenues with a total of 30 new time-limited spaces. The City will begin updating parking signage next Friday, April 3. Increased parking enforcement will begin the week of April 6. These parking updates are the first phase of a broad plan to improve the parking experience for Civic Center visitors. A second phase, planned for the summer, would convert Bonita Avenue between Vista Avenue and Oakland Avenue to one-way traffic (northbound toward Oakland Avenue). This would eliminate the school dropoff zone on Bonita and add additional ADA, time-limited, and employee parking spaces on the street. The City Council approved the parking changes for the Civic Center in May 2025 after several months of discussion. A community survey was completed by more than 500 residents. All the green curbed spaces on Bonita (diagonal and parallel) will become time limited parking - mostly 2 hours.

articles.text: Search for 2 suspects underway Piedmont police are searching for two suspects after a woman was assaulted during a residential robbery on Tuesday, March 24, in the 400 block of Scenic Avenue. According to authorities a male resident returned home around 12:25 a.m. to find his front door broken open and two suspects inside. The man safely fled the residence and called 911. A woman inside the home was asleep in her bedroom at the time of the home invasion. She reported that two suspects entered her bedroom, demanded cash, and assaulted her when she was unable to comply. Police reported the suspects then “ransacked” the home. When the police arrived, the suspects had fled. Using Flock Safety camera technology, officers identified the suspects’ vehicle leaving the area. The vehicle was located within an hour in Oakland and was towed for evidence. The suspects are described as two Black men in their early 20s, approximately 5’10” and 6’0” tall, wearing gray and black hoodies. Piedmont police released a statement on their social media, warning residents to secure their homes and be aware of their surroundings. “With the recent warm weather, we know many residents are opening windows and spending more time outside. Please continue to lock doors and windows, use exterior lighting when possible, and promptly report suspicious activity,” said the Piedmont Police Department. Anyone with information, or who may have witnessed suspicious activity in the area around that time, is urged to contact the Piedmont Police Department at (510) 420-3000. Using Flock Safety camera technology, officers identified the suspects’ vehicle leaving the area. The vehicle was located within an hour in Oakland and was towed for evidence. Please continue to lock doors and windows, use exterior lighting when possible, and promptly report suspicious activity,” said the Piedmont Police Department.
